title: Learning Task-relevant Representations for Generalization via Characteristic Functions of Reward Sequence Distributions

problem.claim: Visual distractions in high-dimensional observations can harm learned representations in visual reinforcement learning and degrade generalization across environments with the same tasks.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Characteristic Reward Sequence Prediction (CRESP), which extracts task-relevant information by learning reward sequence distributions.
CRESP uses an auxiliary task that predicts characteristic functions of reward sequence distributions to learn task-relevant representations.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe CRESP as a novel approach.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that experiments demonstrate significantly improved generalization performance on unseen environments.
The authors report that CRESP outperforms several state-of-the-art methods on DeepMind Control tasks with different visual distractions.

narrative_sequence.summary: Generalization across environments with the same tasks is important for visual reinforcement learning applications.
Visual distractions can damage learned representations and reduce generalization performance.
CRESP learns reward sequence distributions to extract task-relevant information because reward signals are task-relevant and invariant to visual distractions.
CRESP predicts characteristic functions of reward sequence distributions to approximate high-dimensional distributions and learn task-relevant representations.
Experiments reportedly show improved generalization on unseen environments and better performance than several state-of-the-art methods on DeepMind Control tasks with visual distractions.

source_observation.claim: Reward signals are described as task-relevant in reinforcement learning and invariant to visual distractions.

interpretation.claim: Learning representations from relatively invariant task-linked signals may reduce sensitivity to nuisance variation in observations.

application.claim: For visual reinforcement learning systems, consider auxiliary representation-learning objectives based on reward sequence information when visual distractions are a major source of distribution shift.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether reward sequence information is sufficiently informative or invariant for tasks beyond the reported setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide quantitative performance values or experimental details.
The abstract does not specify the compared state-of-the-art methods or the full range of DeepMind Control tasks and visual distractions.
The abstract does not report computational costs, implementation details, or failure cases.
